item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-27286d8dc2339f5b","start_unit":216,"end_unit":218,"fact_summary":"The Tribunal Electoral's final computation recorded Andrés Manuel López Obrador as the majority winner of the 2018 presidential election with 30,110,327 votes out of 56,601,874 validly counted votes, and documented totals by state and overseas voting.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.8","8B.1"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"Pre-2023 institutional baseline relevant to López Obrador's constitutional mandate and electoral succession context; does not itself establish conduct during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The official electoral tribunal record directly attributes the result to López Obrador's candidacy and coalition.","limitations":["The record concerns the 2018 election, not a 2023 event.","It establishes electoral legitimacy and result, not the fairness of every campaign practice or later democratic conduct."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":29,"end_unit":30,"fact_summary":"A Nexos review reported that by 2023 López Obrador had not met stated goals on economic growth, security, corruption, or poverty reduction: it cited 2023 GDP growth of 0.6%, more than 173,000 cumulative homicides, 71.6% of respondents perceiving much or regular corruption, increased extreme poverty and poverty by income, a rise to 50.4 million people without health access, increased educational lag, and lower PISA results than in 2018; it also stated that he failed promises that the executive would not dominate other powers and would not use public budgets electorally.","question_ids":["2B.3","2B.8","2B.9","2B.10","5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.7","5B.9","5B.10","6B.2","6B.5","6B.6","6B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.8","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers 2023 outcomes and end-of-period assessments, though the source is an analytical review published in 2024 and some figures are cumulative or based on 2022 data.","ruler_attribution":"The review attributes the stated promises, policies, and executive conduct to López Obrador and his administration.","limitations":["The passage is an analytical synthesis rather than a primary administrative dataset.","Several indicators have different reference years and causal attribution is not independently established in the supplied extract."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":31,"end_unit":32,"fact_summary":"Nexos reported that by December 2023 López Obrador described the Segalmex diversion of more than 15 billion pesos as the only corruption case in his government, despite documented warnings about procurement irregularities beginning in 2019 and accumulating evidence through subsequent years; the review identified 32 corruption cases for 2023 and alleged selective protection of close collaborators and insufficient accountability.","question_ids":["5B.5","5B.7","7B.1","7B.2","7B.4","7B.6","7B.7","7B.9","7B.10","8B.8"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly addresses the 2023 corruption record and the president's response to evidence available during his term.","ruler_attribution":"The source directly attributes the public statement and protective posture to López Obrador; the documented procurement warnings and cases are attributed to investigative organizations and media.","limitations":["The extract summarizes reported cases and does not provide final judicial findings for each case.","The claim of selective protection is the source's analytical conclusion."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":32,"end_unit":32,"fact_summary":"A Nexos analysis stated that from 2019 to 2023 the López Obrador government attacked or weakened judicial and autonomous oversight institutions through proposed reforms, budget reductions, denunciations, threats of political trial, and partisan appointments; it contrasted institutional resistance by the INE and, later, the Supreme Court with the CNDH's alleged loss of independence, and described Arturo Zaldívar's Supreme Court leadership as overly accommodating to presidential priorities.","question_ids":["4B.2","4B.4","4B.5","4B.10","7B.5","7B.6","7B.7","8B.4","8B.5","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Covers 2019-2023, including the target year, but is a retrospective analytical assessment published in 2024.","ruler_attribution":"The analysis attributes the institutional pressure, proposed reforms, and political strategy to López Obrador and his movement; institutional responses are separately identified.","limitations":["The extract presents the author's interpretation of institutional behavior.","It does not enumerate every appointment, budget change, or court decision."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":34,"end_unit":37,"fact_summary":"Nexos analyses reported that the administration's austerity and anti-corruption agenda did not produce lower spending, greater efficiency, or less corruption; instead, it centralized decisions, reduced administrative capacity, reassigned resources outside legislative control, and intensified unilateral budget modifications. The review cited 2019-2022 executive overspending of 1.014 quadrillion pesos and redirection of 4.203 quadrillion pesos, while a separate five-year estimate described more than 5 quadrillion pesos redirected and major presidential projects costing almost three times initial estimates with limited public detail.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.5","5B.6","5B.7","5B.10","7B.3","7B.7","7B.9","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The analyses cover the administration through 2023, while several expenditure figures end in 2022 or aggregate 2019-2023.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes the centralization, budget reallocations, austerity policy, and presidential projects to López Obrador's executive.","limitations":["The figures are reported by analytical articles and are not reproduced from the underlying budget tables in the supplied extract.","The source uses Mexican large-number terminology that may create translation ambiguity; the quoted magnitudes should be checked against the underlying units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":35,"end_unit":36,"fact_summary":"A Nexos account described López Obrador's governing model as prioritizing loyal, disciplined officials over technically competent administrators and using broad discretionary authority; it stated that the administration's ideological diagnosis of prior reforms lacked empirical support and that austerity rhetoric justified cuts, centralization, and weakened professional capacity.","question_ids":["4B.5","5B.2","5B.6","5B.7","6B.4","6B.5","6B.9","7B.5","8B.2","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Describes the governing model in force during 2018-2023 and is relevant to 2023 administrative execution.","ruler_attribution":"The source directly attributes the stated governing conception and administrative choices to López Obrador.","limitations":["This is an interpretive account of appointments and administrative philosophy, not a complete personnel audit.","It does not identify every official or distinguish all departments."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":33,"end_unit":34,"fact_summary":"A Nexos economic analysis stated that Mexico's 2021 tax revenue was 16.7% of GDP, below the Latin American average of 21.7%, and warned that weak public revenues and rising current expenditure threatened sustainable public finances; it linked the problem to the broader inherited and continuing fiscal structure rather than to one isolated 2023 decision.","question_ids":["5B.3","5B.7","5B.10","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Provides structural fiscal context for 2023 using 2021 comparative data and a December 2023 assessment.","ruler_attribution":"The source discusses López Obrador's administration and the fiscal trajectory during his term, but the cited tax statistic is national and not exclusively attributable to him.","limitations":["The statistic predates 2023 by two years.","The extract does not establish how much of the fiscal gap resulted from López Obrador's decisions versus inherited structural conditions."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":33,"end_unit":33,"fact_summary":"Nexos reported that by December 2023 Mexico's economy had experienced prolonged stagnation, with GDP per capita expected to be lower than in 2018, and identified weak revenues and growing current spending as obstacles to sustained development; it also noted potential upside from nearshoring and the T-MEC.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.4","5B.7","5B.9","5B.10","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly concerns the economic position at the end of 2023, while recognizing external opportunities and inherited constraints.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes policy errors and the fiscal trajectory partly to López Obrador's government, while treating nearshoring and T-MEC as external conditions.","limitations":["The passage is an analytical assessment and does not quantify the causal contribution of individual policies.","It reports an expected end-2024 comparison rather than a finalized 2023 GDP-per-capita figure."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":33,"end_unit":35,"fact_summary":"A Nexos account reported that Morena presidential aspirants used extensive public-space advertising during the 2023 succession process without the normal precampaign registration and real-time fiscal controls, and characterized the activity as an early precampaign; it stated that the spending sources were not transparently known.","question_ids":["4B.2","4B.6","4B.8","4B.10","7B.1","7B.3","7B.7","7B.8","7B.9","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 internal succession and electoral-preparation period.","ruler_attribution":"The source identifies the aspirants as Morena figures seeking to succeed López Obrador and describes the governing-party context; it does not prove that López Obrador personally ordered each expenditure.","limitations":["The extract documents the activity and regulatory concern but does not establish the final legal responsibility of López Obrador.","The spending estimates and funding sources are not fully quantified in the supplied units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a235a298a0eaabb0","start_unit":4,"end_unit":5,"fact_summary":"Nexos reproduced assessments that López Obrador repeatedly used presidential morning briefings to discuss elections and promote government works despite INE requests to respect constitutional limits, and that the administration's approach to violence against women appeared stronger in discourse than in implementation.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.7","4B.2","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","6B.8","7B.1","7B.8","8B.6"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The election-related conduct is historical context; the gender-policy assessment predates 2023 and provides background rather than direct 2023 evidence.","ruler_attribution":"The cited assessments directly refer to López Obrador and his government.","limitations":["The election statement concerns an earlier period and should not be treated as a 2023 event.","The gender assessment is an external analysis and does not provide 2023 outcome data."]},{"source_id":"SRC-c641b5035bf7f940","start_unit":10,"end_unit":13,"fact_summary":"Human Rights Watch reported that López Obrador proposed formalizing and extending indefinite military control over federal public security, despite a record of military executions, enforced disappearances, torture, arbitrary detention, evidence fabrication, concealment, and near-total impunity; it also reported that the Army refused to provide Ayotzinapa documents despite express presidential orders, while the Guardia Nacional was already overwhelmingly staffed, equipped, and commanded by military personnel.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","4B.5","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The source is from 2022 but describes the security model and abuses continuing into López Obrador's administration; it is relevant background for 2023, not a complete 2023 incident record.","ruler_attribution":"The proposed military transfer and presidential decree are directly attributed to López Obrador; individual abuses are attributed to military forces and historical patterns.","limitations":["The source predates the 2023 target year.","It reports allegations and institutional patterns, not final findings for every incident.","The passage does not establish that López Obrador personally directed each abuse."]},{"source_id":"SRC-fcaba83085c61c7a","start_unit":17,"end_unit":21,"fact_summary":"Human Rights Watch's 2023 Ayotzinapa documentary record stated that López Obrador promised in 2018 to resolve the disappearance of 43 students but had not delivered answers nearly five years into his term; families and international experts reported that the Army withheld key information, that the expert group stopped work in July 2023 because of hidden evidence, and that the president was perceived as protecting the military rather than compelling cooperation.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.9","3B.10","4B.3","4B.4","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers 2023 testimony, the July 2023 expert withdrawal, and the unresolved case during López Obrador's fifth year.","ruler_attribution":"The promise and command responsibility are attributed to López Obrador; withholding and obstruction are attributed to the Army and senior officials, with the source reporting criticism of presidential protection.","limitations":["The extract includes testimony and documentary narration, not a final judicial determination of presidential responsibility.","The case originated in 2014, before López Obrador's presidency."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":3,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"Freedom House rated Mexico's internet environment Partly Free at 62/100 in 2023 and reported expanding connectivity and robust online political mobilization, but also threats to journalists, probable military-linked illegal surveillance, weakened telecommunications and data-protection regulators, coordinated progovernment manipulation, and a pending cybersecurity bill containing potentially problematic content, privacy, and criminalization provisions.","question_ids":["1B.9","3B.3","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly covers June 2022-May 2023, including the 2023 reporting period.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes regulatory pressure, political manipulation, and surveillance-related concerns to López Obrador's administration or its allies, while separating criminal violence and other nonstate threats.","limitations":["The score is a country-level assessment and not solely a measure of presidential action.","The report states probable links to the military for surveillance but does not conclusively establish López Obrador's personal authorization."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":17,"end_unit":19,"fact_summary":"During the 2023 coverage period, López Obrador failed to fill commissioners for IFT, COFECE, and INAI, weakening their functioning; after a Supreme Court order he appointed COFECE commissioners, but INAI remained unable to operate normally from March 2023 because of a missing quorum, while López Obrador and allies supported dissolving or absorbing independent bodies.","question_ids":["4B.4","4B.10","5B.5","5B.7","6B.5","6B.9","7B.6","7B.7","8B.4","8B.5","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly covers the institutional status during the 2023 reporting period.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes failure to make appointments and support for institutional dissolution to López Obrador and his administration; the COFECE appointments followed a judicial order.","limitations":["The report does not establish that López Obrador controlled Senate votes on every INAI appointment.","It records institutional functioning and reported proposals, not final constitutional outcomes."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":21,"end_unit":26,"fact_summary":"Freedom House reported that Mexico had no documented nationwide internet blocking and that courts invalidated disproportionate website blocking and the biometric cell-phone registry, but also described government underreporting of content-removal requests, pressure on journalists, a 2023 cybersecurity bill requiring rapid takedowns and broad criminal penalties, and proposals risking censorship and militarized cybersecurity; no new social-media regulation had passed by the end of the period.","question_ids":["1B.9","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.6","8B.8"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 reporting period and records both existing safeguards and proposed changes.","ruler_attribution":"The proposed cybersecurity law and executive-related regulatory environment are discussed in the López Obrador administration's context; judicial safeguards are attributed to the SCJN.","limitations":["The cybersecurity proposal had not passed, so it is evidence of agenda and risk rather than implemented restriction.","Several content-removal examples involved courts or private actors rather than the president personally."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":29,"end_unit":33,"fact_summary":"Freedom House reported coordinated progovernment online networks and smear campaigns against López Obrador's critics, including more than 20,000 messages targeting Supreme Court president Norma Piña in March 2023; it also reported public-resource-supported InfodemiaMX and a presidential 'Who's Who in Lies' segment accused of presenting biased or false information, while noting no proof that one supportive network was financed by the government or party.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.8","7B.10","8B.3","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Includes specific March-April 2023 activity and continuing patterns from the preceding years.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the presidential communication segment and public-funding context to López Obrador's administration; it identifies other networks as pro-López Obrador but notes that government financing was not proven in at least one case.","limitations":["The evidence establishes progovernment coordination and accusations of misleading content, not personal direction of every account.","Some findings rely on investigative reporting and platform assessments rather than completed legal findings."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":37,"end_unit":40,"fact_summary":"Despite threats, harassment, and digital manipulation, Mexican users continued to operate independent outlets and mobilize online; in February 2023 large demonstrations opposed López Obrador's proposed electoral Plan B, and the Supreme Court invalidated the reforms in May and June for legislative-procedure violations.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.3","4B.4","4B.10","7B.6","7B.7","8B.9"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 mobilization, judicial review, and institutional resistance.","ruler_attribution":"The electoral reforms are attributed to López Obrador; mobilization is attributed to civil society and opposition users, and invalidation to the SCJN.","limitations":["The fact demonstrates functioning opposition and judicial checks, not that López Obrador voluntarily accepted or supported them.","The extract does not state his response after the rulings."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":41,"end_unit":45,"fact_summary":"Freedom House reported that Mexican law formally protects speech, press freedom, privacy, access to information, and internet access, and that the judiciary remained generally independent enough to invalidate the biometric registry and right-to-be-forgotten rules; however, López Obrador criticized the newly elected Supreme Court president and his administration sought to weaken existing safeguards, while proposed cybersecurity penalties threatened broad online expression.","question_ids":["3B.8","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.6","7B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 country-report period, with some cited judicial decisions from 2022.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes criticism and policy proposals to López Obrador and attributes protective rulings to the independent judiciary.","limitations":["The passage combines constitutional guarantees, judicial decisions, and executive proposals; these should not be treated as equivalent forms of implementation.","The report does not show whether all proposed criminal provisions were enacted."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":50,"end_unit":55,"fact_summary":"Freedom House reported extensive Pegasus surveillance of journalists, human-rights defenders, and undersecretary Alejandro Encinas, with evidence suggesting military responsibility and a secret military intelligence unit lacking legal basis; López Obrador denied or minimized the allegations, authorities were slow to investigate, and INAI ordered SEDENA to search for and disclose spyware contracts in January 2023.","question_ids":["3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","3B.9","4B.3","4B.4","4B.9","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 reporting period, including the January INAI order, March evidence, and May Encinas reporting.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes denials and minimization to López Obrador and evidence of surveillance to military structures; it does not establish that the president personally ordered individual operations.","limitations":["Several allegations were reported as probable or suggested rather than finally adjudicated.","The source reports slow investigation but does not provide a final accountability outcome by the end of the period."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":57,"end_unit":60,"fact_summary":"During 2023 the INAI lacked a quorum and had nearly 6,000 pending cases after the Senate failed to appoint commissioners; López Obrador and allies supported dissolving the institution, while the Supreme Court later allowed it to meet with four commissioners. Existing law permitted extensive metadata retention and real-time geolocation access subject to judicial safeguards, and a 2023 biometric identity bill raised privacy concerns.","question_ids":["1B.9","4B.4","4B.9","4B.10","6B.5","6B.9","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Directly covers the 2023 reporting period and distinguishes executive-legislative obstruction from later judicial repair.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes support for dissolving INAI and the broader institutional posture to López Obrador and his allies; judicial restoration is attributed to the SCJN.","limitations":["The metadata law predates López Obrador and includes judicial-warrant requirements for historical data.","The biometric identity bill was proposed or pending, not established as implemented policy in the extract."]},{"source_id":"SRC-26432e3d86aa471d","start_unit":60,"end_unit":69,"fact_summary":"Freedom House documented severe threats to online journalism: 696 journalist aggressions in 2022, 196 digital attacks, multiple murders and arbitrary detentions, police assaults, threats, doxing, and a 2023 vehicle arson against a digital-media director; it also reported a 2023 hack of a feminist outlet and a major military data breach caused by unpatched systems, with one officer arrested in March 2023.","question_ids":["1B.3","1B.9","3B.1","3B.2","3B.3","3B.4","3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","3B.9","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","7B.6","7B.7","8B.3","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The source gives 2022 baseline data and specific incidents through April 2023, relevant to the target period.","ruler_attribution":"The violence is attributed to organized crime, local officials, police, and other actors; the military cybersecurity failure and state accountability context concern institutions under López Obrador's administration.","limitations":["Not all attacks were perpetrated by federal authorities or personally attributable to López Obrador.","The data include events before 2023 and do not provide a complete annual 2023 total."]},{"source_id":"SRC-dc57e4e634723e04","start_unit":74,"end_unit":81,"fact_summary":"An AP retrospective reported that López Obrador developed a strong personal connection with many Mexicans, held about 1,400 long televised morning briefings, and relied on cash social programs; it also reported that he frequently made statements contradicted by officials or crime figures, that projects were often ill-planned, and that his administration expanded military control over law enforcement and economic assets while weakening independent regulators, oversight agencies, media conditions, and democratic checks.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.6","4B.5","4B.6","4B.10","5B.1","5B.6","5B.7","5B.10","6B.1","6B.7","6B.9","6B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.8","7B.10","8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Retrospective published after the 2023 period and focused on the full six-year presidency; relevant to end-of-period assessment but not a contemporaneous 2023 source.","ruler_attribution":"The AP account directly attributes the communication style, social programs, military expansion, institutional changes, and disputed statements to López Obrador.","limitations":["The article is a retrospective synthesis and includes post-2023 developments.","Several claims are attributed to analysts or critics and should not be treated as final causal findings."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":["SRC-a915a0062ce7a0c9","SRC-5afa63ce1a03d25d","SRC-3f72a8da81a910c3","SRC-a8a7776a8899889f"],"batch_limitations":["The supplied sources are uneven: several are search or country landing pages, retrospective analyses, or reports published after 2023 rather than contemporaneous primary records.","No supplied document materially addresses nuclear weapons, arms control, proliferation, interstate war, or other existential-risk governance by López Obrador in 2023.","Most adverse claims concern institutional patterns, allegations, or analytical conclusions; the supplied extracts do not provide final adjudications for every alleged act.","The election tribunal record concerns the 2018 mandate and is included only as relevant constitutional and electoral context."]}
